title: Nine thousand open flow mappings followed by 140,608 lines of distinct keys
notes: The input is never closed, so it is an error: a syntax error at the end of the input, or a limit error if the reader refuses the nesting first. No result is allowed. The keys of the innermost mapping are 140,608 different names (`xaaa` to `xZZZ`, none of them a number, boolean or null), so a reader that rejects duplicate keys still reads every line. A reader that looks at every open flow mapping for each line does about 1.3 billion steps here. The time limit is 100 seconds and is a hang guard, not a measure of cost: the readers that answer need between 3 and 15 seconds here, on a quiet machine and on one or two cores, so the limit sits far above all of them. At this size the cost does not separate readers: the reader this case was built for, whose time was quadratic (nine seconds for a five megabyte input of this shape), finishes inside the limit and passes, and only a reader that hangs goes over it. The input is a stored file of under a megabyte, which is what keeps this case in the fast set. The cost is checked by safety/deep-flow-mappings-200000-then-many-lines-unclosed, the same lines under 200,000 open mappings, which sits in the slow set and which readers whose cost grows faster than the depth times the number of lines do not finish inside its limit (two libraries were measured); a reader that only checks every open mapping once per line may still finish inside it. The memory bound is the real check here. See safety/shallow-flow-mappings-then-many-lines-unclosed for the same lines at depth 100. The limits are the robustness requirement of the kit, not a rule of the specification. Input: nine thousand `{`, then each name followed by a comma and a line break.

provenance.reference: A reader whose time was quadratic here: each line was checked against the pending implicit-key slot of every open flow mapping, taking nine seconds for a five megabyte input of this shape.
